askTitle: What the guideline says about diagnosis – to show your doctor
askNote: Each point sums up a passage of the international FD/MAS guideline (2019), with the original wording underneath. Show them to your doctor and ask whether they apply to your child.
askP1: In most cases FD/MAS can be diagnosed clinically, after an evaluation of the whole body: bones, hormones, soft tissue and skin.
askQ1: Which of these areas have been assessed in our child so far, and is anything else planned?
askS1: In most cases, the diagnosis of FD/MAS can be made clinically after a complete staging evaluation for skeletal, endocrine, soft tissue and dermatologic features.
askP2: A single bone lesion without skin or hormone findings can resemble many other diseases and usually needs confirmation under the microscope.
askQ2: Is it a single lesion in our case, and what is the diagnosis based on?
askS2: Isolated monostotic bone lesions without accompanying skin or endocrine findings include a wide differential diagnosis and diagnostic uncertainty and usually require histological confirmation.
askP3: When the diagnosis is in question, the guideline recommends a genetic test for the GNAS mutation, especially for a single lesion in the skull once other signs of the disease have been ruled out.
askQ3: Is the diagnosis certain in our case, or is this test worth considering?
askS3: A genetic diagnosis is recommended where the diagnosis is in question. This especially applies to isolated/monostotic lesions in the skull, after exclusion of other associated skeletal and/or extraskeletal features…
askP4: A negative genetic test from blood cannot rule out FD in a single bone; a positive result is informative.
askQ4: If the blood test was negative, what does that mean for us?
askS4: Use of blood for mutation analysis cannot exclude the diagnosis of monostotic FD, but a positive result is informative.
askP5: If a diagnostic biopsy is taken, the tissue should be sent fresh or fresh frozen so that it can be tested for GNAS. A result can still be falsely negative if the sample contains normal tissue, and the biopsy may then need to be repeated. Testing is also possible on paraffin-embedded samples, but a false negative is then more likely.
askQ5: If a biopsy is planned, how will the sample be handled, and could it be tested for GNAS?
askS5: Diagnostic biopsies should be processed as fresh or fresh frozen material to enable genetic testing for GNAS mutation. False negatives may occur if the biopsy contains normal tissue and the biopsy may need to be repeated. Mutation analysis can also be performed in paraffin-embedded samples although false negatives are then more likely.
askP6: A biopsy is usually needed only in unusual or questionable cases, or when a malignant tumour is suspected.
askQ6: Is a biopsy needed in our case, and if so, what should it settle?
askS6: Biopsy with histological evaluation of suspected bone disease is usually only necessary in unusual or questionable cases, and/or if malignancy is suspected.
askSource: Quotations are from: Javaid MK et al., Best practice management guidelines for fibrous dysplasia/McCune-Albright syndrome, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2019;14:139 (PMID 31196103). The summaries and questions were written by the GeneQuest Foundation; the guideline authors have not reviewed or approved them.

safetyBold: Everything here is a starting point for a conversation with your doctor — not a recommendation.
safetyBody: We show official guidelines plainly; “to consider” recommendations and AI drafts always carry a label, a rationale, and a “discuss with your doctor” note. Your doctor makes the decisions — we help you know what to ask.
unusualTitle: Your case doesn't fit this description?
unusualBody: An unusual course, results that contradict each other, or doctors who disagree — write to us. We read every message. We will try to point you to papers and doctors who have described similar cases, and help you put together questions for your doctor. We don't diagnose and we don't judge treatment — that stays with your doctor.
unusualNote: Your message goes to the GeneQuest Foundation's inbox ({{email}}). Please don't attach medical records or anything that identifies your child — a few sentences are enough to start.
